name: Neural and Evolutionary Computing

papers.title: Multi-objectivization Relaxes Multi-funnel Structures in Single-objective NK-landscapes
papers.abstract: This paper investigated the impacts of multi-objectivization on solving combinatorial single-objective NK-landscape problems with multiple funnel structures. Multi-objectivization re-formulates a single-objective target problem into a multi-objective problem with a helper problem to suppress the difficulty of the target problem. This paper analyzed the connectivity of two funnels involving global optima in the target and the helper NK-landscape problems via the Pareto local optimal solutions in the multi-objectivized problem. Experimental results showed that multi-objectivization connects the two funnels with global optima of the target and the helper problems as a single bridging domain consisting of the Pareto local optimal solutions. Also, this paper proposed an algorithm named the multi-objectivized local search (MOLS) that searched for the global optimum of the target problem from the global optimum of an artificially generated helper problem via the Pareto local optimal solutions. Experimental results showed that the proposed MOLS achieved a higher success rate of the target single-objective optimization than iterative local search algorithms on target NK-landscape problems with multiple funnels.

papers.title: Compressing probabilistic almost-linear recurrent networks without refitting
papers.abstract: Can a compressed recurrent network reuse its learned noise model? We applied finite-horizon balanced truncation to ten probabilistic almost-linear networks on delayed recall. Reducing 64 states to 32 without refitting met forecast tolerances for seven networks when balancing included rectifier inputs, compared with one using the readout alone. Including rectifier inputs improved agreement with the parent's mean-centred forecast distribution on all ten networks, with a median reduction in discrepancy of 65%. Compared with random directions, rectifier inputs reduced centred divergence on six networks and mean forecast error on all ten. Both full and reduced networks underestimated uncertainty on weak cues.

papers.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
papers.abstract: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.

papers.title: Is Chaotic Dynamics Enhancing Particle Swarm Optimization? An Anytime Performance Assessment
papers.abstract: The search dynamics of particle swarm optimization (PSO) can be driven by random or chaotic values. We study if there are performance differences between random and chaos if distributional equivalence of the used sequences is observed. Therefore, we consider an anytime performance assessment which quantifies the fraction of runs reaching a given target value within a specified numerical budget. Furthermore, we connect quantifiers of the chaotic dynamics to performance metrics of the anytime analysis. The results show that once the underlying distributions are controlled, deterministic chaotic sequences yield no general or consistent advantage over random sequences. Performance differences arise most prominently from the underlying distribution, but also from search-space dimensions, benchmark targets, and numerical budgets. We also find potential budget-dependent advantages under specific parametrization of chaotic maps and distribution settings.

papers.title: Geometry, masking and selection in Differential Evolution and SOMA on quantum state manifolds
papers.abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) and the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA) generate new candidates through vector arithmetic: they subtract population members, scale the difference, and mask coordinates. Many practical search spaces are not vector spaces, however. Rotation angles are periodic, normalized states lie on spheres and projective spaces, and circuit parameters are coupled through the quantum states they produce. We present a systematic study of how such geometry affects the core operations of DE and SOMA. Keeping the operators and selection rules fixed, we replace only their geometric primitives and separate the effects of difference construction, masking, and selection in a large paired numerical study covering textbook manifolds and variational quantum problems. Geometry-consistent differences make full-crossover (CR = 1) DE significantly better on 16 of 31 non-Euclidean configurations, with no significant deterioration, and the advantage persists when the measured computational cost of each variant is taken into account. The effect is largest where ordinary subtraction misrepresents distances between candidates: success on periodic synchronization rises from 44% to 100%, and on a positive-definite matrix problem from 1% to 99%. On six- qubit variational eigensolvers, shortest-path angular differences reduce the mean final loss by 90% for about 3% extra runtime. The improvements come with two contrasting diversity patterns, more effective population contraction or preserved population diversity, so higher acceptance rates do not necessarily indicate better search. Crossover masks interact with geometry: they can favor cheaper retractions and can increase the distance moved in quantum-state space when circuit parameters are coupled. These results give practical rules for designing population-based optimizers on non-Euclidean and quantum search spaces.
